newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin doctor says Yeltsin recovering well.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin doctor says Yeltsin recovering well.

text.p: The Kremlin's chief doctor said on Thursday that President Boris Yeltsin was recovering steadily from the pneumonia that laid him low last month but cautioned that the 66-year-old Russian leader should limit his workload.

He denied media reports that Yeltsin was suffering from Parkinson's disease, a devastating brain disorder common among elderly people, and said he had dropped hard drink in favour of beer and light white wine.
"His (Yeltsin's) condition is satisfactory," Sergei Mironov, the head of the Kremlin medical centre, told Ekho Moskvy radio. "He is gaining physical strength and increasing his workload."

The health of Yeltsin, who underwent bypass surgery last year and has been away from work most of the time since being re-elected last July, has become a major public issue in Russia, still battling an economic slump and deep social tensions.
Yeltsin's pneumonia triggered fresh doubts about his ability to lead the vast country and drew renewed calls for him to stand down.
Mironov said Yeltsin's pneumonia, which affected both lungs, had been serious.

"Given that, we consider that his recovery is progressing normally," Mironov added. "Under our rules a person in such a situation should stay in hospital for a month or even six weeks followed by two or three weeks of rehabilitation."
He said Yeltsin was expected to recover his strength sufficiently by March 6 to deliver his annual state of the nation address at a joint session of both parliamentary chambers.
But he made clear that in the meantime doctors were doing their best to limit the activities of the president, who is now spending most of his time in the Gorky-9 country residence outside Moscow.
"We recomend that he makes no more than three trips a week to the Kremlin," Mironov said. "One day in the Kremlin should be followed by a day of work in the country residence."
He said this recommendation was made at least partly because Yeltsin tried to use his trips to the Kremlin to escape his doctors' scrutiny and take on too much work.
"This (Yeltsin's work) is not my sphere," Mironov added. "(But) we can give recommendations and urge pauses when his (working) meetings stretch beyond several hours."
He said that doctors had also imposed limits on Yeltsin's intake of alcohol, adding that the president accepted them.
"We are compromising to some extent but things don't go further then beer and very light dry wine," he said. "Boris Nikolayevich is not insisting (on stronger drinks)."
Yeltsin has long been known to enjoy a drink or two.
Mironov said that Yeltsin had regained some of the weight he lost during his long illness.
"During the preparations for surgery we recommended that he lose some weight," he said. "The loss of weight can also be explained by lack of appetite during his heavy pneumonia."
"I can say now that in the last days Yeltsin gained around 1.5 kg (3.8 lb) and he now weighs 86 kg (215 lb)," said Mironov.
